relationships.description: The engine-enforced integrity constraint groups the fields it constrains (e.g. the columns of a composite unique key or CHECK expression) without owning them, so each field persists if the rule is dropped.
relationships.evidence: The DDL or collection validator (a CHECK, UNIQUE, PRIMARY KEY or FOREIGN KEY clause, or a $jsonSchema 'required'/'properties' entry) names the field in its column list or expression.

relationships.description: A referential constraint propagates a delete or update on the parent record into the dependent collection, so the engine removes, nulls or rewrites the referencing records there.
relationships.evidence: The foreign key definition in the schema migration declares ON DELETE CASCADE, SET NULL or ON UPDATE CASCADE and names the referencing table or edge collection as the dependent side.

relationships.description: The storage-level constraint is the mechanism that makes a stated data-integrity need hold, such as 'every order must reference an existing customer' or 'email addresses must be unique', so the need is met regardless of which application writes.
relationships.evidence: A requirement ID appears in the migration comment, constraint name or traceability matrix linked to the constraint, and a test that attempts a violating write shows the engine rejecting it.

notes: cascades-to fits only referential constraints with ON DELETE/UPDATE actions; CHECK, NOT NULL and unique rules never cascade, so this relationship should be limited to foreign-key rules. Satisfies overlaps with the governance predicate enforces-requirement; the spec should pick one predicate for constraint-to-requirement traceability.
